# Sigma-Algebra as Magma of Sets

## Definitions used

**Magma of sets.** Let $X$ be a set and $\mathcal P(X)$ its power set. Let $I$ be an index set; for each $i\in I$ let $k_i$ be a cardinal and let
$\phi_i:\mathcal P(X)^{k_i}\to\mathcal P(X)$ be a mapping (for $k_i=0$, $\mathcal P(X)^{0}$ is the one-point set consisting of the empty tuple $()$, so $\phi_i$ is just a choice of a subset of $X$). A system $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ is a *magma of sets for $(\phi_i)_{i\in I}$* iff for every $i\in I$ and every family $(S_j)_{j<k_i}$ with all $S_j\in\mathcal S$ we have $\phi_i\big((S_j)_{j<k_i}\big)\in\mathcal S$.

**$\sigma$-algebra.** A system $\Sigma\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ is a $\sigma$-algebra on $X$ iff
- (SA1) $X\in\Sigma$;
- (SA2) $A\in\Sigma\implies X\setminus A\in\Sigma$;
- (SA3) for every sequence $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$, $\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\Sigma$.

## Claim

Take $I=\{1,2,3\}$, $k_1=0$, $k_2=1$, $k_3=\aleph_0$, and
$$\phi_1(())=X,\qquad \phi_2(A)=X\setminus A,\qquad \phi_3\big((A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\big)=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n .$$
Each $\phi_i$ is a well-defined mapping into $\mathcal P(X)$: $X\subseteq X$, $X\setminus A\subseteq X$, and a union of subsets of $X$ is a subset of $X$.
Then for every $\Sigma\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$:
$$\Sigma \text{ is a }\sigma\text{-algebra on }X\iff \Sigma\text{ is a magma of sets for }(\phi_1,\phi_2,\phi_3).$$
Hence the concept of $\sigma$-algebra is an instance of a magma of sets.

## Proof

By definition, $\Sigma$ is a magma of sets for $(\phi_1,\phi_2,\phi_3)$ iff the following three conditions hold:

- (M1) ($i=1$) For every family indexed by $j<0$, i.e. for the unique empty tuple $()$ (whose "entries are all in $\Sigma$" vacuously), $\phi_1(())\in\Sigma$. That is: $X\in\Sigma$.
- (M2) ($i=2$) For every $1$-tuple $(A)$ with $A\in\Sigma$, $\phi_2(A)\in\Sigma$. That is: $A\in\Sigma\implies X\setminus A\in\Sigma$.
- (M3) ($i=3$) For every family $(A_n)_{n<\aleph_0}=(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ with all $A_n\in\Sigma$, $\phi_3((A_n))\in\Sigma$. That is: $\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\Sigma$ for every sequence in $\Sigma$.

These are literally (SA1), (SA2), (SA3). Therefore $\Sigma$ satisfies (SA1)–(SA3) iff it satisfies (M1)–(M3), i.e. $\Sigma$ is a $\sigma$-algebra iff it is a magma of sets for $(\phi_1,\phi_2,\phi_3)$.

## Remarks on variant definitions

1. *Countable families instead of sequences.* If (SA3) is phrased as "$\bigcup\mathcal A\in\Sigma$ for every countable $\mathcal A\subseteq\Sigma$", it is equivalent to (SA3) given (SA1), (SA2). Indeed, sequences give countable families $\{A_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ with the same union. Conversely, if $\mathcal A\subseteq\Sigma$ is countable and nonempty, there is a surjection $n\mapsto A_n$ from $\mathbb N$ onto $\mathcal A$ (repeat elements if $\mathcal A$ is finite), and $\bigcup\mathcal A=\bigcup_n A_n\in\Sigma$ by (M3); if $\mathcal A=\varnothing$ then $\bigcup\mathcal A=\varnothing=X\setminus X\in\Sigma$ by (M1), (M2).

2. *$\varnothing\in\Sigma$ instead of $X\in\Sigma$.* If (SA1) is replaced by $\varnothing\in\Sigma$, the two versions are equivalent in presence of (SA2), since $X=X\setminus\varnothing$ and $\varnothing=X\setminus X$. One may equally use the nullary operation $\phi_1(())=\varnothing$.

3. *Countable intersections.* If a definition additionally demands closure under countable intersections, this follows from (M2), (M3) via De Morgan: $\bigcap_n A_n=X\setminus\bigcup_n(X\setminus A_n)$; alternatively add a fourth operation $\phi_4((A_n))=\bigcap_n A_n$ with $k_4=\aleph_0$ (well-defined as a subset of $X$ since the index set $\mathbb N$ is nonempty).

In every variant, the $\sigma$-algebras on $X$ are exactly the magmas of sets for a suitable family of operations on $\mathcal P(X)$. $\blacksquare$
